title: Leaving full-time music for the Whitney Bank
summary: Dawson says he took a job at the Whitney Bank in 1917 and kept playing night jobs.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Who were you playing with when the September storm occurred?

Well I was practicing with Rene and then after the storm in 1915 I went to work, then I went to work at the Whitney Bank. After the crash came about and things got bad, you know, things got dull, so the law came up, I'd work, fight and go to jail. That was around 1917, you see. And so I just got tired of walking around. I just said, well I met a fellow over there and he was poor at the Whitney Bank and I asked him that he could have had an opening there for me and he said yes, he'd get me on on the night. And I went to work for the Whitney Bank in 1917 on September 12th. And I've been there ever since.
How long did you have to give up music?

Well I practically didn't give up music, I just kept on playing, you see. But I was, I'd get off at, see when I want to play at night like that, I'd ask the night man, the foreman, to let me off and I'd come back in the morning, you know, and after I'd get off my job and finish up my work, work late. So you could double-dip, huh? Yeah, I'd done that for a long time. Many times my bass was up in the corner in the Whitney Bank, coming off, right off the job, right on my regular jobs at the bank. See, I was doing cleaning up, I was doing poor to work at you. Now, well since I've been there so long, I've advanced up to a messenger now, and I don't have to do all that cleaning up. But at that time, that's all I was doing. We was playing. Night jobs, spot jobs, different places.
